TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA MERKUSII
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Asia, Oceania, Malaysia, Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, Sarawak, Brunei, Philippines, Luzon, Samar, Indonesia, New Guinea, Papua New Guinea, Manus, Milne Bay, Solomon Islands, Guadalcanal, Malaita, Caroline Is., Marshall Is., Gilbert Is., Marianas, Fiji, Samoa, Vanuatu, Santa Cruz Is., Cook Islands, Society Islands, Tuvalu
PHOTOS: hero from inat/merkusii (research-grade wild plants from Micronesia or Malaysia); protologue plates: Griffith 1851 t. 169 (as C. lasioides), Schott 1858 T. 84, Ridley 1925 fig. 216, Hay 1988 Fig. 1; type sheets K000291747 (Griffith 5950), K000499253 (Seemann 653), L 0041899–0041902
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma merkusii (Hassk.) Schott, published in Oesterreichisches Botanisches Wochenblatt 7: 61 (1857).
Lasia merkusii Hassk., Catalogus plantarum in Horto botanico Bogoriensi cultarum alter: 59 (1844). Type: Hasskarl s.n., Java, cultivated in the Bogor botanic garden (holotype L).
Schott's 1857 note, under the heading "Aroideae, sketched by H. W. Schott", says that the plant Hasskarl first made known and placed in Lasia agrees entirely, in habit and in the structure of flower and fruit, with Griffith's later Cyrtosperma, and transfers it. He gives the genus in outline (spathe scarcely twisted, at length withering but persistent; spadix elongate; flowers hexamerous; berries smooth; seed reniform, margined and crested; albumen fleshy; leaves sagittate), contrasts Lasia (spathe tightly twisted, flowers tetramerous, berries muricate, seed almost without albumen, leaves at length pinnatipartite), and separates the two known species: Cyrtosperma lasioides Griff. with a long-cuspidate blade whose basal lobes are parted by a narrow sinus, a spathe 3–6 inches long and a spadix reaching the middle of the spathe; Cyrtosperma merkusii with a cuspidate-acuminate blade whose basal lobes are parted by a wide sinus, a spathe 10–12 inches long and a spadix two-thirds the length of the spathe.² Hay (1988) later showed the two to be one species.⁴
HOMOTYPIC SYNONYMS: Lasia merkusii Hassk., Cat. Hort. Bot. Bogor. alter: 59 (1844)
HETEROTYPIC SYNONYMS: Cyrtosperma lasioides Griff., Not. Pl. Asiat. 3: 150 (1851), the type species of the genus (type Griffith 5950, Malacca, K); Arisacontis chamissonis Schott, Bonplandia 5: 129 (1857) and Cyrtosperma chamissonis (Schott) Merr., Philipp. J. Sci. 9C: 65 (1914), the name long used for the Pacific crop (type Chamisso 54, W); Cyrtosperma edule Schott, Bonplandia 9: 367 (1861) (type Seemann 653, Fiji, BM; K, GH); Cyrtosperma cuspidilobum Schott, C. dubium Schott and C. intermedium Schott, Ann. Mus. Bot. Lugd.-Bat. 1: 284 (1864) (types Korthals s.n., Borneo and Sumatra, L), the last also as C. merkusii var. intermedium (Schott) Engl. (1879); Cyrtosperma ferox L.Linden & N.E.Br., Ill. Hort. 39: 59, t. 153 (1892) (type a Kew plant from Borneo, K); Cyrtosperma merkusii var. giganteum Nadeaud, J. Bot. (Morot) 11: 116 (1897) (type Tahiti, Hitiaa, P); Cyrtosperma bantamense Koord., Bull. Jard. Bot. Buitenzorg sér. 3, 1: 160 (1919), nom. subnud. (lectotype Koorders 41645, Bantam, BO); Cyrtosperma nadeaudianum J.W.Moore, Bishop Mus. Bull. 102: 22 (1933) (type Nadeaud s.n., Raiatea, P)
DISTRIBUTION: Malesia to the Pacific: Borneo, Caroline Is., Cook Is., Fiji, Gilbert Is., Java, Marshall Is., New Guinea, Peninsular Malaysia, Philippines, Samoa, Santa Cruz Is., Society Is., Solomon Is., Sumatra, Vanuatu. Introduced into the Line Is., Marquesas, Nauru, Tokelau-Manihiki, Tuamotu, Tuvalu, Vietnam and Wallis-Futuna Is.¹
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Wild, rare and little used in Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo and Java; the Philippine plants are the unarmed cultivated kind, perhaps escaped; both wild-type and cultivated giants grow in the Solomon Islands. Hay saw no wild material from mainland New Guinea, only cultivated plants on Kiriwina and Manus.⁴ Pollen of the species in early-Holocene, pre-human sediment on Pohnpei shows its natural range was wider than the wild collections suggest.⁶ The Sangihe, Talaud and Siau islands off North Sulawesi grow it as daluga.⁷
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Robust to gigantic herb to 4 m tall. Rhizome short and slender to very large, sometimes globose and weighing up to 70 kg, weakly to freely suckering. Leaves several, sagittate, rarely hastate; petioles c. 40 cm to c. 3 m long, heavily armed, often very heavily with stout conical spines towards the base, to unarmed in cultivated forms; blade c. 30 cm to 1.3 m long and to c. 80 cm wide, armed or not beneath, held more or less horizontally to vertically with the posterior lobes down; posterior lobes somewhat exceeding the anterior; primary venation of the anterior lobe curvinerved in small plants to pinnate in large ones; posterior midribs naked in the sinus for c. 5 cm.⁴
INFLORESCENCE: Inflorescence solitary on a peduncle similar to but usually shorter than the petioles, like them with a geniculus at the top that turns blackish on drying. Spathe very variable in size, colour and shape, 2.5 to c. 30 cm long, white, yellow, green or purple, the pale ones usually with purplish streaks outside, rolled back to deflexed to erect with increasing size, the erect ones somewhat constricted above the level of the spadix apex; spadix 2–24 cm long, equalling or exceeding half the length of the spathe, sessile to stipitate, the stipe free or adnate to the spathe. Flowers hexamerous; ovary 1–2-ovulate; stamens exserted from the tepals at male anthesis. Fruit reddish orange, sessile, 1(–2)-seeded. Seed campylotropous, almost circular in profile to shallowly kidney-shaped, 5–11 mm long, brown, with about three raised, warty longitudinal crests to sparsely and irregularly warty and faintly crested.⁴
ECOLOGY: Lowland swamp forest, open swamps and cultivation, mostly near sea level; in cultivation dug pits and taro swamps on atolls and high islands.⁴ Herbarium records range from sea level to about 1,800 m, with a median near 10 m.⁵
DISTRIBUTION MAPS: Hay 1988 Fig. 2 (Malesia; additional localities further east in Oceania).
ETYMOLOGY: Hasskarl's epithet honours Pieter Merkus (1787–1844), Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies when the Bogor garden was catalogued; the 1844 entry itself carries no dedication. Griffith's lasioides means Lasia-like, after the genus in which Hasskarl had placed the plant. The generic name is from the Greek kyrtos, curved, and sperma, seed, for the strongly curved seed, as Schott spelt out in 1858.⁸
NOTES:
1. The giant swamp taro of the Pacific: babai in Kiribati, pulaka in Tuvalu, baba on Guam,⁹ ape veo on Raiatea,¹⁰ daluga in the Sangihe islands,⁷ sampi gede in Sundanese Java.¹¹ Grown for its enormous corm, in the past a staple of atolls where little else will grow; Hay judged it a crop becoming obsolete in favour of Colocasia and Xanthosoma, but one whose origin, variation and development deserve inquiry as an early Melanesian and Polynesian crop.⁴
2. The species as Hay circumscribed it covers a wide range of form. Spathe poise follows its size relative to the spadix: a small spathe is stretched during expansion and deflected, a large one stands erect. Wild plants are heavily armed throughout the range; the unarmed, massive forms are cultivated selections, whose seeds are larger, less ornamented and less curved and whose fruit set is lower. None of these characters correlates with another well enough to separate wild from cultivated plants formally.⁴
3. Where it was domesticated is unresolved. Either the species has a natural range split between West Malesia and Papuasia, like its closest relatives on Bougainville, the Louisiades and the Lorentz River, and was taken into cultivation in the Solomons or the west or both; or the seemingly wild plants of the Solomons are relics of the earliest, still spiny, introductions from the west, such as are grown in the Trobriands and on Manus.⁴
4. Nicolson suggested the cultivars be surveyed for polyploidy; Hay found the chromosome and stem-morphology data too scant to settle it.⁴ Genetic work has since begun in North Sulawesi.⁷
5. Koorders could find no authentic material of Lasia merkusii at Bogor in 1919 and matched his Bantam plant to it on Hasskarl's description and the shared Sundanese name Sampi; his manuscript name bantamensis appears only in a footnote.¹¹
6. Engler's Pflanzenreich account of C. merkusii and C. edule mixed in New Guinea material that belongs to C. cuspidispathum and C. macrotum, and his fig. 6, captioned C. edule, is C. cuspidispathum.⁴
7. In cultivation the plant is the one Cyrtosperma most often seen, in botanic gardens and among growers, and the giant unarmed forms exceed 3 m.

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA JOHNSTONII
PHOTOS: hero from inat/johnstonii (a well-grown clump showing the mottled petioles; wild plants from the Solomons exist among the research-grade records); plates: Ill. Hort. 27 Pl. CCCXCV (1880, as Alocasia Johnstoni), Bot. Mag. t. 8567 (1914); type sheets K000499263, K000499264
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma johnstonii (W.Bull ex T.Moore & Mast.) N.E.Br., published in The Gardeners' Chronicle n.s. 18: 808 (23 December 1882).
Alocasia johnstonii W.Bull ex T.Moore & Mast., Gardeners' Chronicle n.s. 5: 603 (6 May 1876), in the report of Mr Bull's six new plants at the Brussels exhibition: "a species having purple, mottled stalks, furnished with short prickles arranged in groups, and arrow-shaped, erect, dark green leaves veined with red", said to come from New Guinea.¹² Hay (1988) had taken Bull's 1878 retail list as the place of publication and chose a Kew sheet as lectotype;⁴ Hay (2020) showed the basionym was validly published in 1876 and neotypified it.⁵
N.E. Brown's 1882 note records the first flowering in Europe, at the Compagnie Continentale d'Horticulture, Ghent, of the plant "which Mr. W. Bull introduced from the Solomon Isles, and sent out as Alocasia Johnstoni": peduncle like the petiole and armed with clusters of spines in an interrupted spiral; spathe ovate-lanceolate, acuminate, slightly convolute at the base, about 5 inches long, apparently brownish; spadix 2 inches by a quarter inch, brownish, flowering from the apex downwards; perianth of six free segments; six free stamens with exserted white anthers; ovary ovoid-oblong, one-celled, with two or sometimes one anatropous ovule fixed to the side of the cell. He calls it "the first Cyrtosperma that has been cultivated in European gardens".²
HOMOTYPIC SYNONYMS: Alocasia johnstonii W.Bull ex T.Moore & Mast., Gard. Chron. n.s. 5: 603 (1876)
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Known for a century only from cultivation and said to have come from the Solomon Islands; the one field record Hay could find was a juvenile from open country at Hapan on Buka Island, labelled Caladium.⁴ The first wild-collected specimens were gathered in 2013 in the New Georgia group, Western Province, Solomon Islands.⁵ Herbarium records otherwise come from botanic gardens on four continents.⁶
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Gigantic suckering herb to c. 3 m tall, usually with one crown strongly dominant but eventually forming a clump of large crowns. Leaves several together, hastate to sagittate; petioles to 2.5 m long, irregularly and obliquely mottled white, green, brown and pink, heavily armed with the spines coalescing into oblique combs; costae bright pink in young plants, later the blades blotched reddish brown beneath and the costae green to brown; posterior lobes somewhat exceeding the anterior, to c. 70 cm long.⁴ Bogor plants measured by Alderwerelt had petioles 125–250 cm long, the prickles partly scattered and partly in obliquely transverse lines forming spiny crests, and blades green with a red-brown margin and minute carmine dots beneath.⁷
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle similar to but shorter than the petioles. Spathe deeply and narrowly boat-shaped, 9 to c. 40 cm long, rather abruptly more deeply and narrowly concave in the upper portion, erect, dark purple outside, pale dirty yellowish green within; spadix 7–25 cm long, with a short free stipe, somewhat glaucous; flowers hexamerous; anthers exserted at male anthesis; ovary 1–2-ovulate. Fruit and seed unknown to Hay in 1988;⁴ fertility is the subject of Hay's 2020 note.⁵
ECOLOGY: Lowland; the Buka juvenile came from open country and the 2013 collections from the New Georgia group.⁴ ⁵ In cultivation grown both as a terrestrial and as an aquatic, the aquatic plants the larger.⁷
ETYMOLOGY: Named by William Bull's nursery for a Johnston who is not identified in the 1876 report or in Brown's 1882 note; the spelling Johnstoni was corrected to johnstonii under the Code.
NOTES:
1. Introduced by William Bull of Chelsea in the 1870s, exhibited at Brussels in 1876 as an Alocasia "from New Guinea", figured in colour by André in 1880 as Alocasia Johnstoni,⁸ and first flowered in Europe at Ghent in 1882.² Brown published it again with a plate and description in the Botanical Magazine in 1914, calling it the only Cyrtosperma then in cultivation.⁹
2. Phenotypically very variable with age and treatment: young plants show the brilliant pink costae, well-grown ones the dark blotching beneath, and an established clump carries the whole range of inflorescence sizes at once among crowns of different sizes.⁴
3. Diploid, 2n = 26.¹⁰ The inflorescences are protogynous and self-sterile, and plants bearing several at once fail to set seed, so Hay concluded the species is either sterile or physiologically self-sterile and that all cultivated plants are probably a single clone.⁴ Hay (2020) revisits origin and fertility with the wild material now known.⁵
4. "Widely distributed in living botanical collections, but too slow growing to be of much commercial horticultural interest" was Hay's verdict in 1988;⁴ it is now a sought-after collectors' plant and most iNaturalist records are of cultivated specimens.³
5. A traditional medicine in Thailand; its flavonoid glycosides, rutin and isorhamnetin-3-O-rutinoside, and their hydrolysis products show antioxidant, antiproliferative and anti-inflammatory activity in vitro.¹¹

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA MACROTUM
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Indonesia, Papua, West Papua, Papua New Guinea, Morobe, Madang, Milne Bay, Western Province
PHOTOS: hero from inat/macrotum (wild plants, Indonesian Papua); plates: Beccari 1882 Malesia Tav. XXIV figs 1–6, Hay 1988 Fig. 12; type sheets K000291749 (Versteeg 1108), L 0041897, L 0041898
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma macrotum Becc. ex Engl., published in Bullettino della R. Società Toscana di Orticultura 4: 295 (1879), as "macrota".
Type: Beccari P.P. 619, West Papua, Andai (lectotype FI, chosen by Hay 1988). The protologue also cited Beccari's Batanta plant, which Hay made the holotype of C. beccarianum, and a D'Albertis gathering from the Fly River that mixes a leaf of this species with an inflorescence of Lasia spinosa.⁴ Beccari redescribed the plant in Malesia in 1882 with figures of the flower, tepals, pistil, fruit and seed.⁵ ⚠ The 1879 Bullettino page itself is not on BHL or Internet Archive and has not been seen for this page.
HETEROTYPIC SYNONYMS: Cyrtosperma syapense Alderw., Bull. Jard. Bot. Buitenzorg sér. 3, 1: 374 (1920) (type a Bogor plant from Mount Syap, BO); Cyrtosperma subulispathum Alderw., l.c. 375 (type Versteeg 1108, Lorentz River, L); Cyrtosperma hastatum Alderw., l.c. 375 and Cyrtosperma consobrinum Alderw., l.c. 375, both placed here tentatively by Hay on their descriptions; Cyrtosperma janowskyi K.Krause, Nova Guinea 14: 216 (1924) (type Janowsky 489, Kurudu Island, L)
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: New Guinea with the Aru Islands and the d'Entrecasteaux group (Normanby and Fergusson), in three disjunct areas: Morobe and Madang Provinces; Milne Bay Province; and the southern side and western tip of Indonesian New Guinea together with Western Province, Papua New Guinea.⁴ Herbarium records run from 7 to 1,100 m, most below 200 m.⁶
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Moderately robust herb to 1.3 m tall; rhizome plagiotropic or very short, to 6 cm in diameter. Leaves 3 to several, hastate to sagittate; petioles divergent from the base, prickly, mottled or not; blades to c. 90 cm long and c. 50 cm wide, usually less, held horizontally or with the posterior lobes down, more or less coriaceous, armed beneath, sometimes heavily, and sometimes on the margins, often with all the blades facing the same way; primary and secondary venation, sometimes very, prominent beneath; costae of the anterior lobe curvinerved to pinnately arranged; posterior lobes markedly exceeding the anterior, asymmetrically ovate to broadly lanceolate, naked in the sinus for up to c. 5 cm.⁴
INFLORESCENCE: Inflorescence solitary, occasionally two in succession, on peduncles similar to and slightly exceeding the petioles. Spathe narrowly lanceolate, to c. 15 cm long and 3 cm wide when flattened, occasionally spiny at the base and along the midline outside, white to yellowish green, brown or purple, its insertion shallowly cup-like or with the margins deflected or shortly decurrent on the peduncle; spadix c. 6–12 cm long and c. 5 mm wide in flower, pale yellow to green, free-stipitate, adnate-stipitate or sessile. Flowers hexamerous or tetramerous or mixed, then sometimes with some pentamerous; ovule solitary, more or less basal; anthers not exserted from the tepals at male anthesis. Fruit sessile, ovoid, orange; seed with a smooth testa, campylotropous, asymmetrical in side view.⁴ The spadix turns to the horizontal as the fruit develops.⁴
ECOLOGY: Lowland swamp forest, lowland rainforest and lower montane forest; 7–1,100 m, mostly below 200 m.⁴ ⁶
ETYMOLOGY: From the Greek makros, long, and ous, otos, ear: the long posterior lobes of the leaf, the "ears" of a sagittate blade. Beccari's name was published as macrota.
NOTES:
1. Highly variable, with complex patterns. Morobe and Madang plants have coriaceous leaves, free-stipitate spadices, hexamerous flowers and a cup-like spathe base; Milne Bay plants have more membranous leaves, spadices with the stipe adnate to the spathe, at least some tetramerous flowers and a spathe shortly decurrent on the peduncle. In the western and southern populations these characters vary independently, so Hay declined to recognise the two eastern entities formally and suggested they are relics of a once continuous lowland species fragmented by Pleistocene drying.⁴
2. The name has a tangled history. Engler published it from Beccari's manuscript in a Florentine horticultural bulletin; Beccari's Batanta plant, cited with it, proved to be a different species; and Alderwerelt's C. hastatum was described with confused citations of von Römer's numbers that Hay could not reconcile.⁴
3. Alderwerelt's C. syapense, described from a young Bogor plant that flowered and fruited in January 1919, had a petiole 25–50 cm long, copiously but not densely prickly and dark green with irregular transverse streaks below, a spathe 10–12 by 3–3.5 cm, pale dirty yellow inside with pale green veins, a yellowish spadix 5–7.5 cm long, tetramerous flowers, and obovoid berries red below and green above.⁷
4. Cyrtosperma prasinispathum was separated from this species in 2024 on its unarmed leaf underside, oblanceolate posterior lobes, elliptic anterior lobe, deflected spathe with an entire margin, leek-green spathe and consistently tetramerous flowers; the two share the Bird's Head region.⁸
5. Type material of C. subulispathum (Versteeg 1108) is imaged at Kew and of C. janowskyi (Janowsky 489) at Leiden.⁶

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA CUSPIDISPATHUM
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Indonesia, Papua, Papua New Guinea, Sandaun, East Sepik, Madang, Western Province, Southern Highlands, Gulf Province
PHOTOS: hero from inat/cuspidispathum (wild plants, Indonesian Papua, with the dangling twisted spathe tip); plates: Hay 1988 Figs 7a–7b; type sheet L 0041893 (Gjellerup 63)
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma cuspidispathum Alderw., published in Bulletin du Jardin Botanique de Buitenzorg sér. 3, 1: 374 (1920), in "New or noteworthy Malayan Araceae II".
Type: Gjellerup 63, Papua, Eta River, upper Tami, 2 April 1910, "shady clayey river side; alt. 85 m" (holotype B, not seen by Hay; isotype L).
Translated from protologue: Petiole about 75 cm long, dark olive- and purple-flamed, sparsely and shortly prickly; blade hastate or sagittate-hastate, about 50 cm long, the anterior lobe oblong, about 20 by 7 cm, abruptly and slenderly beaked at the tip rather than acuminate, the posterior lobes obliquely sublanceolate, about 30 by 10 cm, parted by a right-angled sinus, the posterior costae slightly decurved, bare in the sinus for 0.5–1 cm, unarmed beneath. Peduncle about 85 cm, sparsely prickly below and rather copiously so towards the top. Spathe about 35 cm long, dark violet, sparsely veined, the lower part long-oblong, about 18 by 4 cm, abruptly narrowed into a linear cusp, sharply subulate towards the tip and about as long as the lower part. Spadix stipitate, the stipe about 1 cm, cylindric, about 7.5 cm long and 6 mm thick, greenish white; tepals and stamens six; ovaries cylindric, flattened at the base, rounded and truncate at the apex, one-ovulate.² Alderwerelt added that the New Guinea plants Engler had determined as C. merkusii belong to three species, this one, C. subulispathum and C. hastatum.²
HETEROTYPIC SYNONYMS: N/A. Engler's New Guinea records of Cyrtosperma merkusii and C. edule (1879, 1911) and Krause & Alderwerelt's C. macrotum (1924, as to specimens cited) belong here in part.⁴
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Indonesian Papua (Jayapura: Eta River) and Papua New Guinea in Sandaun (West Sepik), East Sepik, Madang, Western, Southern Highlands and Gulf Provinces.⁴ Herbarium records span 24 to about 760 m, median c. 300 m.⁵
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Moderately robust to gigantic, solitary or rarely suckering herb to c. 4 m tall; rhizome creeping, subterranean, up to 13 cm in diameter but very short because the older parts rot quickly. Leaves 2 to several; petiole brown, green, or mottled in combinations of these with white; armature sparse to dense, the spines, at least in the lower parts of the petioles and peduncles, small, squat, abruptly upturned and easily dislodged; petioles standing subparallel, not distinctly diverging from the base; blade hastate or sagittate, to 1.3 m long, in smaller plants often with the lobes much narrower than long, held with the posterior lobes down and the anterior lobe up, somewhat flaccid, unarmed.⁴
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle somewhat shorter than the petioles. Spathe 17 to c. 100 cm long, clasping in the lower quarter, ovate-lanceolate, in smaller plants erect, with increasing size the apical acuminate portion somewhat reflexed to greatly elongated, spirally twisted and dangling, purple-brown, usually with yellow veins outside and with pale pink to cream streaks towards the midline within; spadix to 18 cm long in flower, with a free, sometimes armed stipe 2–6 cm long. Flowers hexamerous; anthers not exceeding the tepals at male anthesis; stigmas more or less sessile, white turning brown; ovaries predominantly uniovulate, rarely biovulate. Fruit when ripe expelled from the spadix and held there by the stripped-away adaxial epidermis of the tepals. Seed slightly and irregularly ridged.⁴
ECOLOGY: Lowland rainforest undergrowth and regrowth, predominantly on alluvial soils; one collection from lower montane forest on limestone at 500–600 m.⁴ In the Gogol Valley plants in logged regrowth reached the maximum size recorded for the species seven years after clearing, and seedlings establish in one-year-old regrowth.⁴
ETYMOLOGY: From the Latin cuspis, a point, and spatha: the spathe drawn out into a long, tapering cusp.
NOTES:
1. One of the giants of the genus, with C. giganteum and C. timikense; Hay & Imran (2020) compare their C. timikense with this species, which it most resembles.⁶
2. Flowering is protogynous. The stigmas become receptive shortly after the spathe unrolls, in a rapid basipetal sequence over about two days, and remain receptive for about three weeks, each bearing a drop of nectar, unless pollination has occurred. Pollen is released only after the stigmas have ceased; the anthers open by apical pore-like slits and extrude the pollen in coherent rope-like masses, all the anthers of a flower together and in a slow basipetal sequence lasting several weeks along the spadix, the larger the inflorescence the longer the anthesis.⁴
3. Once the nectariferous stigmas stop there is no reward but pollen. Weevils, Trochorhopalus strangulatus, a species ranging from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean, feed on the tissue inside the base of the spathe. The inflorescence emits a faint musty, fruity odour day and night before, during and shortly after anthesis.⁴
4. As the inflorescence becomes an infructescence the geniculus at the top of the peduncle turns the spadix from pointing vertically up to pointing vertically down.⁴
5. Ripe fruits are pushed out of the spadix, presumably by the pressure of their own growth, and dangle from it by the inner epidermis of the tepals, which is stripped away as they emerge; they recall arillate seeds hanging by their funicles. In most Cyrtosperma the fruits stay attached until removed or until the spadix disintegrates; the mechanism is otherwise familiar in Anthurium.⁴
6. The New Guinea specimens Engler cited under C. merkusii and C. edule were not located by Hay and may have been destroyed in Berlin, but from their localities they are almost certainly this species; Engler's Pflanzenreich fig. 6, captioned C. edule, is clearly this plant.⁴
7. In cultivation at Lae the rhizomes suckered into large clumps, which Hay did not see in the wild.⁴ Indonesian growers now cultivate it, and it appears among iNaturalist records as garden plants.³

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA GIGANTEUM
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Indonesia, Papua, Papua New Guinea, Western Province
PHOTOS: hero from inat/giganteum (three observations, 2025–2026, one wild); no type image online (BO); Hay 1988 Fig. 3 map
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma giganteum Engl., published in Nova Guinea 8(1): 249 (1910), in Engler & Krause's Araceae of the Lorentz expedition.
Type: Versteeg 1818, Papua, Lorentz (Noord) River, flowering October 1907 (lectotype BO, chosen by Hay 1988); Versteeg 1141, May 1907, is the other original gathering.
Translated from protologue: Leaf with petiole to 2.5 m long, the adult blade coriaceous, ovate-sagittate, the anterior lobe to about 75 cm long and 70 cm wide at the base, obtuse or apiculate at the apex, the posterior lobes to 1 m or more long and 50 cm wide, bent back, subacute, separated by a deep acute sinus, with about eight distant primary lateral nerves joined into a marginal collective vein, the posterior costae bare in the sinus for about 10 cm. Peduncle to 4.5 cm in diameter, smooth. Spathe ovate-lanceolate with a long acumen, reddish brown, convolute below, about 8 cm across and about 35 cm or more long; spadix dark rose, stipitate for 2 cm, 21 cm long and about 4 cm thick. Stamens 4–5, 3 mm long, on filaments up to 1 mm. Pistil 4 mm long, the ovary with several ovules. Perianth of 4–5 tepals 3.5 mm long. Fruiting spadix to 36 cm long and 9 cm thick. Berries ellipsoid, green, 1.5 cm long and 6 mm thick. Seeds several.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: The Lorentz River basin of southern Papua, where Hay knew it only from Versteeg's two gatherings and Engler's unlocated von Römer 193;⁴ R.J. Johns and colleagues collected it there again in the 1990s, and there are records from Western Province, Papua New Guinea.⁵ Rediscovered in the field by Hay & Imran (2020).⁶
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: A huge plant, poorly known. Leaves with the petiole to 2.5 m long, the blade unarmed and the upper petiole unarmed, the lower part armed with scattered straight spines; blade coriaceous, ovate-sagittate, the anterior lobe to about 75 by 70 cm and the posterior lobes to 1 m or more long.² ⁴
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle to 4.5 cm thick, smooth. Spathe ovate-lanceolate, long-acuminate, reddish brown, convolute below, c. 35 cm or more long and 8 cm across; spadix dark rose, 21 by 4 cm on a 2 cm stipe. Flowers 4–5-merous; anthers exserted from the perianth in a preserved fruiting spadix; ovary with several ovules. Fruiting spadix to 36 by 9 cm, with some 1,300 green ellipsoid berries 1.5 cm long, each holding up to five seeds; the seeds longitudinally crested like those of C. merkusii. By far the largest infructescence in the genus.² ⁴
ECOLOGY: Lowland swamp forest of the Lorentz River, at 10–15 m.⁵
ETYMOLOGY: Latin giganteus, gigantic: the leaves and infructescence are the largest in the genus.
NOTES:
1. Its 4–5-merous flowers, pluriovulate ovary and multi-seeded berries are unique in Cyrtosperma and led Engler to ally it with the African Lasiomorpha senegalensis; the marcescent spathe, the geniculate petiole and peduncle and the free filaments place it in Cyrtosperma proper, and the exserted anthers and crested seeds put it, tentatively, in the Merkusii group.⁴
2. Hay & Imran (2020) reported the species found again in Papua Province, in the same issue of Aroideana that described the second southern giant, C. timikense.⁶
3. Now in cultivation: iNaturalist records from 2025 and 2026 include garden plants.³

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA BECCARIANUM
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Indonesia, Papua, West Papua, Papua New Guinea, Western Province
PHOTOS: no photograph of a living plant in the pack; Hay 1988 Fig. 13 (habit and flowers, from van Royen 4792) is the only illustration; type at FI, not imaged
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma beccarianum A.Hay, published in Blumea 33: 455 (1988), with Fig. 13.
Type: Beccari P.P. s.n., West Papua, Batanta, July 1875 (holotype FI), the specimen Engler had cited in 1879 under C. macrotum. Hay's diagnosis: differs from C. macrotum in the erect posterior lobes of the leaf and the more or less flat, ovate spathe.²
HETEROTYPIC SYNONYMS: N/A. Cyrtosperma macrotum Becc. ex Engl. (1879) pro parte, as to the Batanta specimen.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: South-west and west New Guinea: Batanta and Ramoi in the Bird's Head region, the Lorentz and Digul Rivers and the Merauke area in southern Papua, and the Fly and Palmer Rivers, Kiunga and Lake Murray in Western Province, Papua New Guinea.² Records from 24 to 210 m.⁴
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Feeble to moderately robust herb 40–150 cm tall. Leaves 3–7; sheath papery, fibrous, about a quarter the length of the petiole; petiole sparsely armed to unarmed, rarely rather densely spiny; blade variable, held with the anterior lobe down and the posterior lobes up, usually sagittate; anterior lobe triangular, c. 10 cm long and 8 cm wide at the base; posterior lobes lanceolate, c. 25 cm long and 7.5 cm wide at the midpoint, their midribs naked in the angle of the sinus for up to 4 cm, the sinus 30–100 degrees.²
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle subequalling to exceeding the petioles, mostly with sparser armature, like the petioles variously blotched and marbled green, brown, pink and white, or plain brown or green, often drying greyish. Spathe broadly to narrowly ovate, opening broadly boat-shaped to flat, white, pale pink or pale yellow, the tip acuminate, from 1.8 by 5 cm to 4.8 by 9 cm; spadix sessile, adnate to the spathe for c. 5 mm, 4 by 20 mm in flower and 1.5 by 6 cm in fruit, pale yellow. Flowers tetramerous; ovule solitary. Fruit orange, globose, protruding from the spadix as it swells. Seeds tightly curved, smooth.²
ECOLOGY: Low altitude, in streams and ditches and in the undergrowth of swamp forest and gallery forest, in shade; ecology and leaf form combine to make most individuals rheophytes.² 24–210 m.⁴
ETYMOLOGY: For Odoardo Beccari (1843–1920), the Florentine botanist and explorer of New Guinea who collected the type in 1875.
NOTES:
1. A member of the Macrotum group, distinguished from C. macrotum by the leaf held with the posterior lobes up and the anterior lobe down and by the broad, flat spathe.² Hariri et al. (2024) list it with C. macrotum, C. hayii and C. prasinispathum.⁵
2. The type story: Engler's protologue of C. macrotum cited "Batanta, Beccari" and "Fly River, D'Albertis". Hay found that Beccari 619, the plant actually described and figured in fruit, came from Andai, not Batanta; that the Batanta plant of July 1875 was a different species, which became the type of this one; and that the D'Albertis gathering is a leaf of C. macrotum with an inflorescence of Lasia spinosa.²
3. Small, tetramerous and pale-spathed, it is the species most likely to be confused with C. prasinispathum, whose authors compared their plant only with C. macrotum.⁵
4. ⚠ No photograph of a living plant was found in the sources pulled; the genus-level iNaturalist observations from Indonesian Papua may include it.³

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA BOUGAINVILLENSE
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea, Bougainville
PHOTOS: no photograph of a living plant in the pack; Hay 1988 Fig. 6 (leaf, spathe and peduncle, from Hay 2051); type sheets K000499251, K000499252, A 00025749, L 0041890
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma bougainvillense A.Hay, published in Blumea 33: 441 (1988), with Fig. 6.
Type: R. Schodde & L. Craven 3837, Papua New Guinea, North Solomons Province, Bougainville Island, Maide Gorge, lower southern slopes of the Lake Loloru crater, about 15 miles north of Buin, 14 August 1964 (holotype CANB; isotypes A, K, L, LAE). Hay's diagnosis: differs from C. merkusii in the more or less flat spathe, the twisted stony seed, the vermilion stigma and the glaucous spadix.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Restricted to Bougainville: Panguna, Kieta, Kapikavi and Arawa. Locally abundant there yet unrecorded elsewhere in the Solomon chain; a fragmentary 1931 Waterhouse specimen from "Iru (Mt. area), Siwai" may belong here.² All records are from 1931–1967.⁴
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Robust, usually solitary herb 1–2.4 m tall; rhizome often long and creeping. Leaves 2–5, sagittate; petioles prickly, green mottled with white; spines slender, without conspicuously broad bases, slightly curved, scattered or tending to short comb-like clusters; geniculus up to 14 cm long; sheath papery-fibrous, about a fifth the length of the petiole; posterior lobes 40–75 cm long and 20–30 cm wide, the tips not acuminate; anterior lobe 35–50 cm long and to c. 60 cm wide, with spreading costae.²
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle to 2 m long, usually shorter than the petioles, prickly. Spathe blackish purple to almost white, broadly lanceolate, to 27 cm long and 6.5 cm wide, widely open to the base, somewhat deflected from the spadix and not shielding it from the side, the upper part sometimes falling forward over the spadix. Spadix stipitate for c. 6 mm, the insertion running c. 1 cm up the spathe; fertile part to 11.5 cm long and 1.6 cm wide in flower, purplish to glaucous-blue. Flowers hexamerous; anthers dirty yellow, exserted from the tepals at male anthesis; receptive stigmas bright scarlet; ovules one or two. Fruiting spadix becoming horizontal to pendulous, dark bluish to black. Fruit obpyramidal, c. 8 by 8 mm, orange, truncate at the apex. Seed tightly curved over on itself; seed coat very thick, stony, somewhat rough.²
ECOLOGY: Montane rainforest and regrowth in moist gullies at 600–2,000 m on the actively volcanic, copper-bearing island of Bougainville; possibly restricted to cupriferous soils.² Records at 610–884 m.⁴
ETYMOLOGY: Of Bougainville, the island to which it is confined.
NOTES:
1. The seed is distinctive: campylotropous like the rest of the genus, but with the micropylar and chalazal ends overlapping so that it is helical, and the funicle appears to enter through a hole in the side.² With the heavily ornamented seed coat and the exserted anthers it sits closest to the lowland C. merkusii.²
2. The bright scarlet receptive stigmas and glaucous-blue spadix are unique in the genus.²
3. Bougainville's history since the 1960s has left the species uncollected for decades, and no photograph of a living plant was found.⁴ ⚠

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA BRASSII
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Papua New Guinea, Milne Bay
PHOTOS: no photograph of a living plant in the pack; Hay 1988 Fig. 5 (from a plant cultivated at Lae); type sheets L 0041891, A 00025750
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma brassii A.Hay, published in Blumea 33: 439 (1988), with Fig. 5.
Type: L.J. Brass 28282, Papua New Guinea, Milne Bay Province, Rossel Island, Abaleti, 1 October 1956 (holotype L; isotypes A, LAE). Hay's diagnosis: differs from C. merkusii in the tetramerous flowers, the smooth seeds and the leaves that are rough to the touch when dried.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Confined to Rossel Island at the eastern end of the Louisiade Archipelago; besides the type, Brass 28251, NGF 27090 and a plant grown at Lae.² Records from 1956–1982, at 50 m.⁴
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Robust herb to 2.5 m tall. Leaves 2 to several; petioles spreading out from the base, very prickly with small spines arranged in combs at least towards the base, mottled green and white; blade sagittate, to 120 cm long, held with the anterior lobe up and the posterior lobes down; costae of the anterior lobe pinnate, spreading; posterior lobes with the midribs naked in the sinus for c. 6 cm, to 30 cm wide at the widest point, with acuminate tips; both surfaces of the blade rough (asperous) in the dry state though not when fresh.²
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle similar to but usually somewhat shorter than the petioles. Spathe ovate-lanceolate, to 18 cm long, remaining somewhat constricted above the level of the spadix apex after opening, boat-shaped, blackish purple, with parallel major venation and reticulate secondary venation; spadix with a c. 5 mm free, unarmed stipe, to c. 7 cm long, creamy yellow. Flowers tetramerous; ovaries 1(–2)-ovulate; anthers exserted from the tepals at male anthesis. Fruit ovoid, orange-red. Seed smooth, very faintly longitudinally ridged.²
ECOLOGY: Rainforest on Rossel Island, at low altitude.² ⁴
ETYMOLOGY: For Leonard J. Brass (1900–1971), the Australian botanist of the Archbold Expeditions who collected the type on the Fifth Archbold Expedition in 1956.
NOTES:
1. One of two Louisiade endemics, with C. gressittiorum on Sudest; both are tetramerous members of the Merkusii group, the group otherwise hexamerous.² With C. bougainvillense they are the closest relatives of the giant swamp taro, which bears on the question of where that crop came into cultivation.²
2. Grown at the Lae Botanic Gardens in the 1980s, from which Hay drew the figure.²
3. ⚠ No photograph of a living plant was found.

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA CARRII
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Papua New Guinea, Central Province
PHOTOS: hero from inat/carrii (two observations, one wild 2012, one cultivated 2025); Hay 1988 Fig. 10 (from the type); type sheets BM000958554, BM000958555, L 0041892
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma carrii A.Hay, published in Blumea 33: 450 (1988), with Fig. 10.
Type: C.E. Carr 12307, Papua New Guinea, Central Province, Koitaki, 15 March 1935 (holotype BM; isotypes L, LAE, SING). Hay's diagnosis: differs from all other species of Cyrtosperma in the very broadly ovate spathe convolute at the base and the conoid style.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Central Province, Papua New Guinea: Koitaki, Mafulu, the vicinity of Musgrave, Manumu village and the headwaters of the Kemp Welch River; rare.² Records 1933–1961, at 240–1,250 m.⁴
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Herb to 55 cm tall. Leaves several, hastate, armed on the petiole and on the underside and margins of the blade; petioles to 50 cm long with a sheath 11 cm long; blade to 40 cm long, coriaceous; spines sparse, straight to very slightly curved, to 5 mm long; anterior lobe oblong, gradually acuminate, subequalling the posterior lobes; two anterior costae emerging near the sinus, curvinerved, running to the margin near the tip; posterior lobes broadly lanceolate, their midribs naked in the sinus for c. 3 cm.²
INFLORESCENCE: Spathe broadly ovate, clasping in the lower fifth, c. 12 cm long and to 8 cm wide when flattened, deep reddish brown with yellow, widely reticulate venation that persists as a skeleton around the fruiting spadix; spadix with a 4 mm stipe adnate to the spathe, the fertile part c. 2.5 cm long and 5 mm wide. Flowers tetramerous; anthers not exserted from the tepals at male anthesis; stigmas raised 1–2 mm on the conical apex of the ovary. Fruit ovoid, capped by the style and stigma. Seed smooth.²
ECOLOGY: Lowland and lower montane rainforest undergrowth at 200–700 m.²
ETYMOLOGY: For Cedric Errol Carr (1892–1936), the New Zealand-born orchid collector who gathered the type in 1935 and died of blackwater fever in Port Moresby the following year.²
NOTES:
1. The sole member of Hay's Carrii group: lower spathe convolute, flowers tetramerous, style conical and persisting on the fruit.²
2. The net of yellow veins that remains as a skeleton around the fruiting spadix after the spathe tissue has gone is unique in the genus.²
3. "Cyrtosperma carrii would seem to have horticultural potential", Hay wrote in 1988;² a cultivated plant was recorded on iNaturalist in 2025.³

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA GRESSITTIORUM
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Papua New Guinea, Milne Bay
PHOTOS: no photograph of a living plant in the pack; Hay 1988 Fig. 4 (habit, leaf and flowers, from the type); type sheets L 0041894, A 00025751
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma gressittiorum A.Hay, published in Blumea 33: 439 (1988), as "gressittorum", with Fig. 4.
Type: L.J. Brass 28049, Papua New Guinea, Milne Bay Province, Sudest (Tagula) Island, Rambuso, 11 September 1956 (holotype L; isotype A). Hay's diagnosis: differs from all other species of Cyrtosperma in the hooded spathe.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Known only from the type gathering on Sudest (Tagula) Island in the Louisiade Archipelago, in rainforest on the crest of a ridge at 150 m.²
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Herb to 70 cm tall. Petiole to 60 cm long, the sheath papery and c. 15 cm long, the spines sparse, straight, needle-like, to 3 mm long; petiole variegated green and white. Blade hastate-sagittate, sparsely armed below, c. 30 cm long; anterior lobe subequalling the posterior ones; posterior lobes slender, to 6 cm wide, their midribs naked in the sinus for c. 3 cm, the lesser venation somewhat prominent below; costae of the anterior lobe arising near the sinus, curvinerved, running to the margin near the tip.²
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle similar to but exceeding the petiole, to 90 cm long. Spathe lanceolate, c. 7 cm long, hood-forming in the upper quarter, green, the major venation parallel and distant, the secondary venation reticulate; spadix orange, 4 cm long, with a 5 mm stipe adnate to the spathe. Flowers tetramerous; anthers exserted from the tepals at male anthesis and apparently retracting afterwards; stigmas hardly exceeding the tepals; ovule solitary. Fruit and seed unknown.²
ETYMOLOGY: Commemorates the entomologist and biogeographer J. Linsley Gressitt and his wife Margaret, who died together in an air crash in China in April 1982; it was through Gressitt, at the Wau Ecology Institute, that Hay was first introduced to tropical vegetation. Hay spelt the epithet gressittorum; POWO and the World Checklist correct it to gressittiorum, the genitive plural for two people, and IPNI keeps the original spelling.² ¹
NOTES:
1. The hooded (cucullate) spathe is unique in the genus, and the only species with a green spathe and an orange spadix.²
2. The second Louisiade endemic, with C. brassii of Rossel Island; both are tetramerous members of the Merkusii group.²
3. Still known from the one collection of 1956 as far as the sources consulted show.⁴ ⚠

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA KOKODENSE
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Papua New Guinea, Oro, Central Province
PHOTOS: no photograph of a living plant in the pack; Hay 1988 Fig. 9 (from NGF 23585 and Cheesman 3); type sheets L 0041895, L 0041896, G 00191357
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma kokodense A.Hay, published in Blumea 33: 447 (1988), with Fig. 9.
Type: C.E. Carr 16194, Papua New Guinea, Northern (Oro) Province, Kokoda, 22 March 1936 (holotype L; isotypes B, BM, CANB, SING). Hay's diagnosis: differs from C. cuspidispathum in the mostly straight spines, the armed blade, the spathe not convolute at the base and not long-acuminate at the apex.²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Northern (Oro) and Central Provinces, Papua New Guinea: Kokoda, the Kokoda Trail and Boridi village.² Records 1933–1973, at 350–1,190 m.⁴
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Herb to 1.5 m tall. Blade markedly hastate to sagittate, c. 40–100 cm long in flowering plants; anterior lobe to 30 cm from tip to sinus; posterior lobes obliquely narrowly ovate, to c. 75 cm long, with rather fine and numerous costae diverging from the midribs at about 35 degrees. Petioles sometimes mottled; armature sparse, short, slender, to 4 mm long, straight to upcurved.²
INFLORESCENCE: Spathe to 25 cm long, lanceolate, to 2.5 cm wide, in the lower 5 cm the margins clasping the spadix but not overlapping, deflected in the middle part, spirally twisted in the upper part, the tip not or hardly acuminate, the whole purple, paler within and with yellowish streaks; spadix stipitate for 1 cm, 4.5–5.5 cm long and c. 6 mm wide in flower, cylindrical. Flowers hexamerous; anthers not exceeding the tepals at male anthesis; stigmas brown when dried, papillate; ovary 1(–2)-ovulate. Ripe fruit and seed unknown; Hay expected the fruits to be expelled from the spadix as in C. cuspidispathum.²
ECOLOGY: Rainforest undergrowth and stream sides at around 400 m.²
ETYMOLOGY: Of Kokoda, the type locality in Oro Province, at the northern end of the Kokoda Trail.
NOTES:
1. The second member of the Cuspidispathum group: stamens not exserted, spathe twisted above; it is the smaller plant with straight spines and an armed blade.²
2. Named from material gathered by C.E. Carr in 1936 and by Evelyn Cheesman, who also collected at Kokoda.²
3. ⚠ No photograph of a living plant was found; the Kokoda Trail is well walked and images may exist outside the sources searched.

TITLE: CYRTOSPERMA PRASINISPATHUM
TAGS: Cyrtosperma, Oceania, New Guinea, Indonesia, West Papua
PHOTOS: no iNaturalist or type image; the protologue's Figure 1 (habit, spines, spathe, spadix, flowers, leaf) is CC BY and usable with attribution to Hariri et al. 2024 (protologue pack, Hariri-2024-Webbia-79 p. 293)
PROTOLOGUE:
Cyrtosperma prasinispathum A.S.D.Irsyam & M.R.Hariri, published in Webbia 79(2): 292 (3 September 2024), "Cyrtosperma prasinispathum: a new fascinating Aroid species from Papua, Indonesia".
Type: MRH 777, prepared 14 March 2024 from a living plant at the Bogor Botanic Gardens, Indonesia, Southwest Papua Province, Sorong Regency (holotype FIPIA, isotype BO). The Bogor plants grew from seed, DW1091, collected by D. Widyatmoko at Taman Wisata Alam Sorong at 27 m on 11 June–9 July 2007 and long labelled Cyrtosperma hambalii.²
Diagnosis: geographically associated with C. macrotum but differing in the unarmed abaxial leaf surface, the oblanceolate posterior lobes, the elliptic anterior lobe, the deflected spathe with an entire margin, the leek-green spathe, the yellowish-green to yellow spadix and the consistently tetramerous flowers.²
DISTRIBUTION: New Guinea: New Guinea (Southwest Papua Province, Sorong).¹ ²
DISTRIBUTION NOTE: Known only from the 2007 Sorong collection and its descendants in cultivation at Bogor.²
SPECIES DESCRIPTION: Small herb 21–30 cm tall. Leaves about 5–9 per crown, clustered; sheath 2–4 cm long, brown; petiole slender, 5–25 cm long, brown with black patches, armed with straight, downward- and mostly upward-pointing spines 1–4 mm long, yellowish brown; blade sagittate-hastate, the anterior lobe elliptic, shorter than the posterior lobes, 3.5–12 by 2–6.2 cm, pointing downward, flat in juvenile leaves; posterior lobes oblanceolate, 4.2–17 by 2–5.5 cm, pointing downward, the sinus 60–80 degrees; upper surface dark green, lower surface glaucous.²
INFLORESCENCE: Peduncle 50–73 cm long, brown with black patches, armed with minute straight, downward- and mostly upward-pointing spines 1–2 mm long. Spathe broadly open, lanceolate, deflected, 10.9–11.5 by 2.5–2.9 cm, leek-green. Spadix 35–45 by 6–7 mm, yellowish green turning yellow when mature; stipe 3–6 mm long, leek-green. Flowers bisexual, perigoniate; tepals 4, free, green turning yellow; stamens 4, free, the filaments flat and broad, the anthers c. 0.5 mm long, white, not exserted from the tepals at anthesis; pollen white; ovary one-locular, brown; stigma discoid, sessile, brown.²
ECOLOGY: Lowland forest of the Sorong nature reserve (Taman Wisata Alam Sorong) at 27 m; nothing more is recorded.²
ETYMOLOGY: From the Latin prasinus, leek-green, and spathum, for the glossy leek-green spathe.²
NOTES:
1. The fourth member of the Macrotum group, with C. beccarianum, C. macrotum and C. hayii; the group has a spathe not convolute in its lower part and tetra-, penta- or hexamerous flowers.²
2. Described entirely from living cultivated plants; the authors propose Data Deficient for its conservation status and note that the striking spathe makes it "an important candidate for horticultural plants".²
3. The authors' Figure 1 shows the habit, the three kinds of spine tip on the petiole, the spathe from three angles, the spadix and immature flowers, and compares the leaf with those of C. macrotum and C. hambalii.²
4. With C. hayii it brings the genus to 15 species, 14 of them east of Wallace's Line.²
